newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt plays down EU attack, key ally livid.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt plays down EU attack, key ally livid.

text.p: The Italian government sought on Monday to play down a politically damning European Union report which cast doubt on its chances of getting the economy into shape for the launch of the single European currency.

But opposition parties used the EU document to savage Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government, while the coalition's hardline ally, the Communist Refoundation, furiously accused Brussels of meddling in internal affairs.

European Union finance ministers criticised Italy at a meeting on Monday for lax controls on state spending in 1996 and told Rome it still had much to do if it wanted to reduce its budget deficit in a lasting fashion.

Prodi, speaking to reporters while on a visit to Bosnia, said that despite the strongly worded document, Italy would still be a founder member of the European economic and monetary union (EMU) when the single currency was adopted in 1999.
"There is no doubt about that," he said.
The opposition Freedom Alliance grouping of centre-right parties said the EU document was further proof that the government was pursuing the wrong economic policies.

"This government plans to overhaul public finances with measures which have a short-shelf life, with accountancy tricks and with one-off measures," said former foreign minister Antonio Martino, economics spokesman for the centre-right Forza Italia party.

Italy's 1996 deficit/GDP ratio was 6.7 percent. It has pledged to reach this year the three percent goal laid down by the Maastricht Treaty for EMU hopefuls and has introduced some 78 trillion lire ($46.7 billion) of deficit cuts in the last five months to meet that target.
However, many of the recent measures will expire at the end of the year and the EU demanded more sustainable spending cuts.
"These are things that have been said time and time again but the government is pretending not to hear," said Pier Ferdinando Casini, head of the small centrist CCD party.
Economists say that if heavily-indebted Italy is to stay below the three percent deficit/GDP threshold, social spending must be chopped.

Government representatives are due to meet union leaders for the first time on Tuesday to start what promise to be lengthy negotiations over a reform of welfare spending, especially the loss-making state pensions system.
But both unions and Communist Refoundation are adamant that social expenditure cannot be reduced. Refoundation politicians accused EU ministers of trying to force Rome into radical pension revisions.

"We must show the European Union that Italy is a sovereign state, that it knows how things are, that it knows how to take its own decisions and does not need advice or directives from other people," said Refoundation president Armando Cossutta.

Italy is one of the most enthusiastic supporters of the single currency within the EU, but its determination to become a founder member, despite its huge debt mountain, has alarmed many of its European partners.
"The Italian government should put an end to the present excessive deficit situation as rapidly as possible," the EU report on Monday said.
